utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kickert.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please be seated. The cross-examination by Mr. Lukic will now continue. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Kickert. My apologies again for the fact that you had to come back just for my sake, but I will finish soon. Can you please focus on the time when you wept to Gornje Obrinje with Finnish forensics team. With the leave of the Chamber, because we found this document quite late yesterday, but it is a document which goes to this incident and this is Exhibit D197. We distributed hard copies to the parties because it was not uploaded into e-court and we informed the Prosecution yesterday that we would use the document today with the permission of the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document was sent last night at 10 to midnight and it's in violation of your order as well that you made in August last year of when documents for cross-examination should be disclosed, and we object to the use of this document for that reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, does that mean you don't accept Mr. Lukic's explanation that he only found it quite late yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think the same standards should apply to both parties. We also only found the document we weren't allowed to use, we only got it the day before I wanted to use it, and we weren't allowed to use it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you didn't tell us that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I never got to that point, Your Honour. I think I did tell you that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That you only found it the day before?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: We only received it from the witness when he came in for proofing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, well, that's a rather different situation. Yes, I understand the difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller, we don't accept that the situations are comparable. Yesterday's document involved a failure to ask us to alter the 65 ter list. You have obligations to intimate the terms of that list not only to the Defence but to the Court. The Rule that you're relying on is our practice of requiring intimation a certain time before the document is used, and that clearly is a Rule that's open to variation depending on the circumstances in which the document comes to light. Now, I'm assured by Mr. Lukic that this has only been found yesterday, and in light of that, the situation can't be compared to the one that we faced yesterday. You were urged repeatedly in the past to interview your witnesses in good time, not immediately before they gave evidence and to apply properly for variation of the 65 ter list. So we do not treat the two situations the same, and we will in this case allow the use of this document. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. For your convenience we provided you with the translation of the document and the original. It's actually a draft translation done by our team.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kickert, did you manage to go through the document?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite yet, if you could give me two more minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Sure. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we continue?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We found this document yesterday through the system where we normally obtain the Prosecution documents. Unfortunately, we were unable to find a translation and we had to make one ourselves, and I hope that you are able to understand what this is all about. As you can see, the document shows that the SUP of Pristina informed the Belgrade MUP and the Pristina MUP at once that the district court in Pristina sought assistance from the MUP of Republic of Serbia and the Pristina MUP in order to secure the exhumation of corpses in Donje Obrinje, and that's on the date of the 10th of December, 1998. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that on this occasion you, in fact, agreed with the district investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, there was -- my understanding of the whole procedure was that the district judge, Mrs. Marinkovic, could accompany us, but I was not aware that we would have a tail of 20 armoured vehicles and APCs and police cars. Because I knew the situation on the ground and I knew this was an area where the UCK was; and had I known before, I would -- I personally would not have said -- agreed to start out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that the investigating judge was the one who issued the order for the scene to the attended and for the exhumation to be carried out?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our understanding was that the Finnish forensic experts had whole freedom to do their investigations. They have been the day before without any investigating judge, without any Serbian police. They have been at the site of Gornje Obrinje to prepare the site of exhumation. So for us -- for the Finns and for us it was no necessity to be accompanied. I understand that the Serbian government insisted on it, but for us to do the work of the Finnish forensic experts, it was not necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true, and this transpires from the document, that the investigating judge did not want to proceed this time without police security?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were the Serbian authorities duty-bound to secure the site and to provide security for you and the Finnish forensic experts pursuant to the agreements stipulated with your organisation?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: From our point of view there was no security threat to us because we had contacts with the KLA. They gave us assurances we can do the exhumations. We also were in touch with the families of the victims, so that we had also this security, that they would not object to the fact that we would be exhuming the bodies of their relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time Gornje Obrinje, which was in the Drinjacka region was under the control of the KLA and this was the month of December of 1998.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: As it says also in your report that there were KLA people seen with long-rifled guns, this was also our understanding. This is why for security reasons we did not continue because we would have - we the Finns and myself- we would have been in the cross-fire between KLA and MUP. So the only decision we could take was not to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In fact, the KLA never left the area we are discussing, but we will get back to that in a minute or two. Are you aware that the police were unable to decide as to whether to escort you or not if the investigating judge had issued an order for the police to, in fact, provide the escorting and security services to you?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we didn't ask for the security escort --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise. This is what I'm asking you. Are you aware of the fact that pursuant to the Yugoslav and Serbian legislation, it is not up to the police to decide whether they would set out to secure an exhumation site; rather, it is in the domain of the investigating judge. The police can only honour the orders issued by the investigating judge. Are you familiar with this?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with this legislation, but you probably are.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] I hope so. [Interpretation] Thank you. That the KLA was active in the months of August and September in the area as well was something that was experienced by the KVM observers when on the 14th of September they hit an anti-tank mine. Do you recall that in the village of Likovac in the Srbica municipality an all-terrain vehicle of a Chevrolet make which was owned by the Canadian Embassy in Belgrade hit a mine and the vehicle was containing members of the mission for Kosovo and Metohija, they hit an anti-tank mine that was laid by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that incident very vividly. It was Canadian KDOM, and because it was armoured they were lucky enough to survive and they were even lucky enough that because their satphone was destroyed also in the incident that they went up to a hill and got a signal for their cellphone and only through that they could ask for help. And later on there was also a car of the ICRC who -- in that same particular area driving on a mine -- I mean, as I explained, I'm not a specialist but it must have been a pretty heavy mine, and there was one local doctor killed at that particular second incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the second incident took place on the 30th of September, 1998, according to the documentation I have as well as according to your report number -- or rather, which is Prosecution Exhibit P557, dated the 30th of September. On page 1, the last paragraph mentions the second incident precisely, or rather, you mention it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, 557, first page.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, a dead and two seriously wounded and the last page, it's just a -- and I also talk about the Canadian KDOM.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. The documentation also shows that attacks were carried out against the police in the months of August and September on several occasions. I should like to hear from you whether we can agree that the KLA was active in this area throughout the time and after the September of 1998 they recaptured the entire area where you, in fact, found them in the month of December?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was difficult for us to say which area was sort of recaptured or lost or taken, but I think I can agree with you that also on -- our understanding was in the Drenica region the KLA was active throughout. And I think also -- I remember also the -- when Gornje Obrinje happened that I think special forces of the MUP drove on a mine and killed several officers, and that was our understanding that this may have been -- may have triggered the incident in Gornje Obrinje that some colleagues went on a rampage afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you then agree with me that the reason why an investigation and the exhumation of corpses in Gornje Obrinje could not be carried out before the arrival of the Finnish forensic experts was the very presence of the KLA in the area.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: For us it was the presence of the MUP. We would -- as the Finnish forensic experts, we would have done the exhumations and we would have filmed it with video and everything, we would have been able to do the exhumations. But if the judge said -- insisted that she wanted to be there and she wanted to be there, it could only happen if the MUP accompanied her, that rendered the whole operation impossible, and this was the reason I was complaining also to the Serbian Minister of Justice, that if you really want us to do the exhumations to establish the facts, then please let us do our job on our own.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your explanation. My question to you was whether the KLA presence in the area made it impossible for the Serbian forces to carry out an exhumation investigation before that date independently.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean the -- at the time when the whole allegation of the Gornje Obrinje incident is that it was performed or committed by Serbian forces, so they were in the area, but I don't think they were there permanently. I don't know about the attempts of the Serbian authorities to investigate the incident; I'm not aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please turn to your document marked P564. This is the report dated the 11th of September, 1998. Under item 4 you speak of the fact that nobody came to the Serbian humanitarian centre, and the conclusion was drawn that none of the civilians had returned to that area by then. Relative to this, my question is as follows: Are you aware that the KLA rigorously punished every Albanian they learned had been taking humanitarian aid from Serbia, and this was, in fact, the main reason why the Serbian humanitarian aid centres were scarcely visited by Albanians or not at all. Did you in your work come across any reports speaking to that effect?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of any such reports, and to begin with, if there are no returnees it's logical that these centres will not be frequented, anyways.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm speaking of situations where returnees went back to their homes, but even then they did not visit these centres because they were prohibited from taking any aid from Serbia. Were you aware of this? Were you also aware of the fact that all those who did go to collect aid were styled as collaborationists?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't heard any reports on this when I was working there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kickert, the point I think that's being made here is that you can't make a judgement from the absence of people at the humanitarian aid centre that there is -- that no one has returned --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, there are two separate questions there, and the one that really concerns us is obviously whether or not people had returned. Now, what do you say on that point more broadly than simply focusing on the humanitarian aid centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in my report I state that -- that is independent of the humanitarian aid centre, that the Albanian population of Decani had not returned. And independently of that, that the humanitarian aid centre of Decani was open, it was equipped, but it was not frequented. I do not make this connection here that -- that -- that the population was there and did not frequent it. I say there is a humanitarian centre in Decani and it was not frequented, point full stop. And then I say, The Albanian population has not returned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did have in -- in Orahovac we had also humanitarian centre and people returned, but even there the Albanian population would not frequent -- maybe that goes in the direction of your -- even there Serbian humanitarian centre was not really frequented. I was a couple of times in Orahovac to see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that the area of Decani was a place where civilians successively were returning too, perhaps not at the time you were drafting this report?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can agree with you is that this was an area of fighting and that there was a number of IDPs and that they were shifted around, IDPs, and they sort of fled the areas of fighting; that I can agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please turn to your document P558. You yourselves expressed distrust towards some sections of the translation that was made, and I would like to clarify certain matters with you. Confusion may arise from the fact that there are four spares or some words have several meanings and it may not even be due to the translators themselves but to the imprecision. In paragraph 2 you say that your colleague met with the prefect for the region of Djakovica. In view of the translation we received, I have to ask you this, this also due to the fact that the word "prefect" in our language is used in quite a different context. I have to ask you this, therefore; this is a civilian person, is it not? This is a civil authority, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, it was not in uniform, so I -- yeah, civilian person.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. [Interpretation] Your colleague met with four security coordinators there, as you put it. Would you agree with me that since this term was used at this trial to denote persons who provided local security -- let us clarify this. At any rate, we are talking about Albanians who were armed by the municipality. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was -- I cite my British colleague, and he told me that he met four of them in uniforms which had special markings and that they would be provided the very next day with side-arms. So he did not see them armed, but they would be provided. And I stated yesterday, at an earlier meeting where I was present the deputy said that he was not aware that they would get uniforms or side-arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I said this because of the translation so that we could link this with the local security. That was actually the term used in this courtroom. Thank you. My colleagues have established with you already that it had not been easy to find these people because they had been accused of collaboration with the Serbian state on the part of their Albanian colleagues. I should like to ask you in this connection the following: Did you ever learn during the course of your work that these people were often the target of KLA attacks and that many of them had been abducted and killed?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this specific person security coordinators, no, but from early 1998 there were many reports that the KLA had not only targeted police but had also targeted what they said were collaborators. And in the beginning I remember they were postmen, they were forest workers who were killed and -- were allegedly killed by the KLA. That indeed what was put forward in the public, in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I appreciate that in that time, due to the information you had at your disposal, you said that this information lacked seriousness. But did you later, during the course of your work, find out that these local security units had been set-up, organised, and that they were functioning, the local security service?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I said yesterday, we did not follow that anymore because it was overtaken by events and then KVM and a lot of these issues, so we did not follow that up anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you never found out that in over 70 villages this formation of armed Albanians had been organised and was acting in an organised fashion? And that is in the area of Djakovica alone, 70 villages.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number 70, I read in one of the -- those reports. Again, I don't know who put it forward to us, but apart from that being mentioned to us, this number, we have not seen or experienced it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page -- but we do not have an updated transcript from last night so I only have three-digit numbers. It is 122, line 15 of yesterday's transcript. There you refer to the fact that with Baton Haxhiu you went to attend some KLA meetings, and we know that you used his services as interpreter. Do you know whether he and other interpreters faithfully interpreted what you were being told by KLA representatives?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Baton Haxhiu was setting up the meeting in Klecka --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and there he did translate. And since my Albanian is non-existent, I cannot say whether he translated it literally or not. With -- on the other hand, in my meetings in Malisevo with Hashim Thaqi and Kadri Veseli, we spoke directly in German so there was no translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As Baton Haxhiu himself in his testimony in front of this Court, he himself said that he had mitigated the military and militant stances of the KLA in doing his interpreting work, and as you had no way of controlling what he was saying to you, so you wouldn't be aware of the fact that he was changing the substance or actually the tone. However, You're referring Klecka and to your visit to Klecka. Did you on that occasion find out about the camp which was set up and maintained by the KLA in Klecka and about the burnt human bodies that were found in the lime kiln, in the lime pit?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At the time I wasn't even aware where I was in Klecka. I learnt that afterwards -- or when I was there. And about these limestone-burnt bones, I heard out of the press in the moment the Serb security forces took Klecka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just another thing, please. Could you please look at your document number P561, the last paragraph in that document, please. There you say that Milosevic had promised to the International Committee of the Red Cross unrestricted access to prisoners for 24 hours after their detention, that it is seen that 250 out of the 500 recently arrested persons had already been set free. When you talk about these 500 arrested people, does this mainly refer to people who had been arrested on the basis of terrorist activity?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this report, I just cite what Mr. Shattuck told us, so to be honest I don't know which this 500 refers to, which sort of persons they are. We are pressing both sides that the ICRC would get access to detainees also with the KLA because they also took detained people. But concretely on this, I don't know who this 500 number refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Kickert. Thank you very much for your time, and I apologise once again for you having to return here on my sake. I have no further questions for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Just one question in relation to the document Mr. Lukic showed you, 6D197, on the second page if you could have a look at the third-last paragraph which starts with: "Because the investigative judge requested ..." It then says: "The investigative judge recommended to the Finnish pathologists that they all return to Pristina, which suggestion they accepted." Was that a suggestion? Did you -- were you actually given a choice where you returned or not - you meaning the Finnish forensic team and everyone who accompanied them?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a bit of a, say, a nervous situation where at a certain moment the Serb police thought that we would continue to Gornje Obrinje without them and they even blocked the left-turn that we would take to go up to Gornje Obrinje, but we had no intention to continue anyways because it became late, A; and B, it was too tense, and as I heard afterwards from my KLA sources, they would have opened fire. So it was a good decision and we were okay with it, to return to Pristina. We would like to had -- to continue without Serb police, but this was not made possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just on that same paragraph the suggestion there was to return to Pristina to negotiate further an agreement to recommence on another day. Was that done?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This -- well, we tried, but the two positions were so diametrically different. The investigating judge insisted that she was present and said, "I can only be present if I have security provided by the Serbian MUP, police." And so this made the whole operation impossible. We asked whether we could do it on our own, as our understanding was that we could pick all sites which were agreed, three on each side, three allegations from each side, and we were not let do that. The investigating judge insisted that she was present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if this is -- I'm sorry. I don't understand that reference that you could pick all sides, three on each side, allegations from each side. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: We -- in all talks to prepare and accept the Finnish forensic team we agreed on three sites each. First it was four sites each, meaning four allegations from the Serb side of massacres, like Klecka, like Golubovac and then I think Ratis and I don't know what the last fourth was. But then we boiled it down to three on each side. It was on the sort of Albanian accusation side, it was Gornje Obrinje, it was Golubovac. We did -- the Finns eliminated Prekaz because, in their pathologist's words, these bodies were old bodies and give less of a -- of knowledge what happened than fresh bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So just to be clear about the day of the -- of this whole business, you actually met again later in the day and tried to work out with Marinkovic a way of doing this?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, and this very same day we even met in Pristina the minister of justice who then referred to -- say, I will consult with Belgrade. So he was not in a position to say, Well, you go ahead without the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And was she willing to move at all and show any sort of understanding of the problem?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No -- Mrs. Marinkovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Absolutely rigid?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely rigid, yeah. I think we -- I think that the Finns had -- in areas which were under Serbian control, they didn't have a problem. In Orahovac, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may be you don't know the judicial set-up well enough to answer this, but was there any way of challenging her position to some higher judge?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a lawyer. I'm just -- I tried to solve things on a political level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Well, Mr. Kickert, that does complete your evidence. Thank you for coming again to the Tribunal to give it, and you're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So who's jumping to their feet?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I think Mr. Stamp will address you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May it please you, Your Honours. Unhappily, we are not able to proceed with the next witness immediately, but we could do so -- propose to do so tomorrow and propose to arrange our witness in such a way so he will be completed tomorrow so he will not stretch over the next week. The witness is a witness that we had problems getting here, but he is here, thankfully, but he just arrived yesterday afternoon and there is, I understand, some debriefing to be done in the Victim and Witnesses Unit which has been done and to get him settled. And we propose to speak with him today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, have you discussed the timing of the witness with counsel for the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We have indicated to them what the situation is and indicated to them that we propose to shorten the time that we planned to use with him so that they would have as much time as necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, if this witness is examined in chief for two hours, will cross-examination be completed tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'm not in a position to assist you on that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which counsel do you think can assist us on that? Mr. Lukic, can you help me, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are we working the full day tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. We are scheduled to have five hours tomorrow, until 3.30. So if the Prosecution have two, you've got three.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'll finish my cross-examination tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you the only one with cross on this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I noticed just one -- it's probably a fairly minor point, but part of the evidence is sought to be tendered as a transcript. Now, I know it is a transcript, but it's not a transcript in the sense of 92 ter, I don't -- quater, I don't think.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, it is not a transcript from this court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. So you may give thought to what the appropriate motion is for the production of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It presumably is just a piece of evidence that he can speak to and confirm the accuracy of or otherwise under Rule 89. But give some thought to that so that we do it properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Thanks for the guidance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we have no option, as you know --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your permission, I believe that now the time is opportune for me to raise a question, and by your leave we need to be in private session for a very short while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 9th day of March, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 9.53 p.m.,
